The paper presents detailed RCS modeling and analysis of simple objects like sphere, cylinder, triangular plate, circular flat plate, and truncated cone using MATLAB Radar Toolbox and POFACET GUI.
For a sphere, the RCS remains constant and independent of frequency for larger radii, but varies with frequency for smaller radii.
The RCS of a cylinder is maximum when it is aligned horizontally with the radar (180 degrees) and minimum at 90 and 270 degrees.
The RCS of an ellipsoid depends only on its dimensions and is independent of azimuth and elevation angle.
The RCS of a triangular flat plate is maximum at 0 and 180 degrees, and minimum at 90 degrees.
For a truncated cone, the RCS has maximum values at 0 degrees and minimum values at 80 degrees, and decreases with increasing frequency.
The RCS of a complex object composed of simple shapes is obtained by vectorially adding the RCS contributions of its individual components.
Swerling models II and IV, which assume a Chi-square probability density function, can be used to model the fluctuating RCS of high-speed debris in low-Earth orbit.
The RCS modeling and analysis techniques discussed in the paper can be applied to determine the structure and characteristics of unknown targets, as well as analyze space debris in low-Earth orbit.
The paper compares the RCS results obtained using MATLAB Radar Toolbox and POFACET GUI for simple objects, showing good agreement between the two approaches.
The detailed RCS analysis of simple and complex objects presented in the paper can be useful for various applications such as military, defense, and satellite communication.
The paper highlights the importance of RCS modeling and analysis in target detection, tracking, and identification for radar systems.
The study includes the analysis of RCS variations with respect to parameters such as size, frequency, and aspect angle for both simple and complex objects.
The paper discusses the limitations of the study, which is focused on objects with deterministic shapes and the combined objects using those shapes.
The Swerling models analyzed in the paper can be used to measure the RCS of high-speed debris revolving around the Earth's surface in low-Earth orbit.
